Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate in the debate on the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) which I submit is a very general motion dealing with the tight money policy as it concerns housing and urban development in this country. I have been one who has been most interested in this field for quite a number of years both before and since coming to this house. I suggest to hon. members that we all know that priorities have their place in the field of housing and urban development. I submit, as a result of condensing a great deal of experience into the short period of six or seven years, that the housing dollar has to be spread where it is most needed.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) stated in his budget address, during these times of tightening up a little on the finances of the country it is natural that one of the fields to be affected is the field of housing generally. It has been the private mortgage field that has been affected most because the private lender has been withdrawing from the field in order to put pressure on the government to bring about an increase in the interest rate on N.H.A. mortgages. The minister in charge of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation knows that I have been opposed to any increase in interest rates on N.H.A. mortgages. In fact, I was opposed to the increase from 6J per cent to 6f per cent.
I suggest that we cannot forget we are experiencing today a dry run so far as mortgage loans from private lenders are concerned because they want to pressure the government into increasing the rate of interest. This cannot be denied, and I feel these people will not deny it.
However, I should like to review briefly the amendments introduced in June, 1964, to the National Housing Act. I doubt that anyone can challenge the fact that in no field has this government shouldered its responsibilities in a more determined fashion than it has in the field of housing. Since these amendments were passed the average Canadian family has been able to build or rent accommodation suited to the needs of that family and their finances. The sweeping changes that were made to the housing legislation also spelled out new hope for those who need to find decent housing for their families, and here I am speaking particularly of the low income groups and the elderly citizens of this country.



groundbreaking ceremonies for a senior citizens home in the city of Hamilton last week. This home is to provide housing for the elderly citizens of the city of Hamilton as well as citizens across the country. The federal government made a 90 per cent loan at low interest rates. These moneys have not dried up, so let us not be fooled into thinking that any tight money policy to control the economy is affecting funds which are made available to help our elderly citizens and low income families. That is not the case.
There is also in the 1964 amendments provision for a program of land acquisition and servicing for public housing purposes in advance of the development of the projects themselves. This new legislation provided loans, again from the federal government, of up to 90 per cent for this purpose. That is why I say that nowhere has this government shouldered its social responsibilities with more determination than in the field of housing, particularly public housing which is geared to low income families and our elderly citizens.
Again, in the legislative amendments of 1964, Mr. Speaker, assistance was made available for non-profit corporation housing. What did this mean? Organizations like the Lions Club, the Kiwanis, to which I belong and which has constructed an elderly citizens home under this legislation in the city of Hamilton, were able in servicing their communities, if they wished to, to construct low-income housing or apartments for elderly citizens with substantial loans from the federal government through C.M.H.C.
To do this a new section was added to provide for 90 per cent loans to non-profit companies, such as service organizations, for housing projects, either used or new, for low-income persons or families who are not eligible for public housing but are still unable to find suitable accommodation at rents which they can afford to pay. Therefore
C.M.H.C. was able to make loans to such companies to finance projects comprising not only self-contained student units but hostels, dormitories or any other combination of accommodation. Again, Mr. Speaker, funds are still available to these non-profit organizations for building this type of accommodation. There has been no drying up of these funds.
What about the case of loans to owners of existing houses in urban renewal areas? For the first time, under the amendments to the urban renewal legislation provision was made for C.M.H.C. to grant mortgages to owners of
Tight Money Policy
existing houses in urban renewal areas. I for one wish to see this legislation extended, I hope very shortly, to all existing houses. These loans are available to owners who apply and there has been no drying up of these funds. The funds are still available. You need only go to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation if you wish to apply for such a loan and C.M.H.C. will take your application.
One of the most important facets of the National Housing Act has to do with university housing for single students and for married students with families. This sort of construction is occurring more and more on the campuses of the country. Again I speak of my own experience with McMaster University in the city of Hamilton where residences are being built for single and married students.
How was this vast growth possible? Under the amendments of 1964 C.M.H C. may grant loans to universities, colleges, co-operative associations and charitable corporations to assist in the construction or acquisition and conversion of accommodation for university students and their families. This accommodation may include the provision of self-contained units as well as hostels and dormitories. For this purpose the maximum amount authorized to be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund was increased to $150 million from $100 million. Provision was also made in this legislation to increase the maximum charge on the consolidated revenue fund for direct lending by C.M.H.C. to $2.5 billion from $2 billion.
What else did this legislation do, Mr. Speaker? It increased loan ratios for N.H.A. insured loans, making it possible for more families to purchase homes with a lower down payment.
I touch on these points briefly to bring to the attention of members of the house and the Canadian public that when a general motion such as this is moved in this house-in fact, I think the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) spoke for only six or seven minutes-which alleges there is a tight money policy in effect, and then arguments are made which leave the impression that there is in existence a tight money policy, the people must be made aware of all facets of the economy of the country. It is incumbent upon the provinces, the municipalities and the people to take advantage of the amendments passed in 1964 relating to public housing and urban development programs, and it is important that they are made aware of the fact that the funds provided under these

May 16, 1966
Tight Money Policy
amendments have not dried up but are still available.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, this house in 1965 approved an amendment which increased the funds provided by the legislation in 1964 by an amount of $300 million in order to carry out the purpose and intent of those amendments. So again I reiterate that there is no shortage of money for urban renewal; there is no shortage of money for public housing; there is no shortage of money for university housing accommodation; and there is no shortage of money to house the elderly citizens of this country. All one need do is to apply for assistance, and the co-operation which I know has been extended by C.M.H.C. to the provincial governments and the municipalities will be similarly extended to all applicants.
There is also no shortage of money for federal-provincial projects with respect to rental housing related to income, the so-called geared to-income housing. The federal government has such funds available and there is no drying up of funds for this purpose.
If I go on at length, Mr. Speaker, about housing and urban development legislation passed in 1964 it is because I want to dispel any suggestions which may have been put forward by hon. members opposite to the effect that there is a general drying up of funds to assist a very important sector of our economy, namely funds for housing for our low-income	groups-the geared-to-income
housing for low-income families and the elderly citizens of the country.
I for one have been greatly interested in the question of urban renewal, and I feel that our provinces and cities have to move to institute a crash program across the country. I have just returned from a 10-day tour across the country as a member of the transportation committee of this house, which has been holding hearings relating to the C.P.R. passenger service. While in the western cities we made ourselves aware of certain problems presently existing.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I, with my interest in housing and urban development, have noted that in cities such as Vancouver and Calgary, and even in smaller cities such as Brandon, Moose Jaw, Medicine Hat and Winnipeg, urban renewal schemes have been undertaken or are in progress. It

would be sad if the impression were left from anything said in this house that funds available for such projects had in fact been dried up by the federal government. That is not the case. I suggest that if a province or a municipality falls down with respect to urban renewal or public housing, for which there is a great need approaching emergency proportions, then it is the fault of such province or municipality. It is a local problem.
I have said in the house before and I now reiterate that the federal government should set up a department of housing and urban affairs to help, together with the provinces and the municipalites, in the solution of the urban problem. I do not ask the government to encroach on other jurisdictions. We must take a broad outlook at the real problem concerning housing and urban renewal. I am sure that if the provinces and municipalities can co-operate under the present legislation there is no reason why they could not cooperate with the present government if a department of housing and urban affairs were set up. We need co-ordination in that respect.
Although housing and urban renewal are the particular prerogatives of the provinces and municipalities, I must nevertheless commend the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), who is responsible for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and for the administration of the National Housing Act, for his action in going across the country when these amendments were passed in 1964 and holding in conjunction with the provinces what were termed "symposiums". These were held not only with the provinces and municipalities but with public service organizations, service clubs and other people across this country and had to do with the legislation which had been passed in 1947. In effect he said to all those attending: Do it and we will help you; the funds are there, so kindly make an application; should you fall down on this job, then you have only yourselves to blame.
I say again that my main purpose in rising to take part in this debate is to dispel the impression left by the generalized amendment now before us with respect to the work which has been done in the fields of urban renewal and public housing, particularly as they affect low income groups and elderly citizens. I want to dispel the impression left by some members opposite who wish to portray across this country that the government has dried up the source of funds to do this important work. That is not the case.

It ill behooves any of us in this house to try to create this impression throughout the country. Public housing is an important field. A lot of work has been done in this field. When I heard the hon. member speak of the tight money policy, and here I am relating my remarks to housing and urban renewal, I at once thought of the niggardly increase from $25 million to $50 million made by the former government in the years from 1957 to 1963 with respect to urban renewal and public housing.
I think hon. members opposite should be the last to talk about a tight money policy as it affects housing and urban development across this country. During the period from 1957 to 1963 the only amendment to the National Housing Act for urban renewal purposes was an increase in the statutory limitation from $25 million to $50 million. If that was not tight money or a retrograde step in urban renewal in this country, I do not know what was.
The bill before the house in 1965 sought to amend the National Housing Act further to increase to $300 million the funds available for purposes of urban renewal and for the purposes of public housing that accompany urban renewal. Passage of the bill by the house assured that Canadian urban renewal projects would boom, as they have done. This program involving housing for our low-income groups-

read the amendment that is before us. It is as follows:

I doubt whether that is a point of order. However, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that the hon. member discussed at great length the amount of money available for the building of residences on university campuses. We do not argue this point. We are talking about direct mortgage loans available to individuals. As a matter of fact, amendments to the National Housing Act permitting universities to build residences were introduced by the Conservative government in, I think, 1961. This legislation provided for an interest rate of 5 per cent, over a period of 50 years, and I am happy to say that practically every university in Canada has made good use of this program.
When talking about money being lent in order to build university residences, and the tight money policy of this government, I should like to point out that if the government were to examine some of the residences being built on university campuses, I am sure they would realize that these residences could be built for less money, be less luxurious, and then more money would be available for the building of homes.
Direct mortgage loans being reduced by 15 per cent is, when compared with the figures of 1965, a very, very serious situation in this country. If my hon. friend from Hamilton West does not realize just how serious this matter is, I would suggest that he sit down with the builders in his community, as I did a few Saturdays ago, and he would realize the problems they face. The builders certainly brought to my attention how serious the problem is. The men in the home building

industry are very, very concerned. Small builders are being put out of business. I refer to the man who builds five to ten homes a year.
The big builder seems to be getting enough mortgage money, but I am concerned about the small builders who face a very, very serious problem. I cannot understand why the minister cut by 15 per cent the money available, the same time as approved lenders were curtailing their loans. Here we have the two lending bodies drawing in the available money all at once. Why did not the minister wait to make his 15 per cent curtailment of funds until after the conventional lenders reduced the amount of money available? But here the two things happened at the same time, creating a drastic and serious situation as far as home building in Canada is concerned.
I do not think there is a member in this house who has not had representations made to him by builders in his community as to the serious problem created by the shortage of mortgage money. I am told that the rich can get mortgage funds but that it is very difficult for the average working man to get a loan. It is true that loans are available for apartment houses. I am told that the large-scale builders can get loans, but the small builder, the man who builds five or ten houses a year is not able to get loans, and this is very serious for him. I am also told that large-scale builders who have reached the saturation point in their own areas are now moving into my own area to build houses, and that this is creating a real problem for the small builder.
I would recommend to the government that first and foremost it should not curtail by 15 per cent direct mortgage loans as compared with last year. They should provide the same amount of money as was available last year, especially at this season of the year. It should not postpone its decision on this until next winter or next fall. Now is the time when builders need and want mortgage money, and if the government wishes to impose this 15 per cent reduction it should postpone its enforcement until later on in the year. Let's get building-now.
There are many areas in Canada in which abnormal expansion and development are taking place. These areas need homes more than other areas. In this connection I think of my own community of Guelph, which is a university town, expanding at a great rate,
Tight Money Policy
bursting at the seams every place one looks. Yet additional loans are not being made available in this area. It receives the same amount of loans as other areas which are not expanding so quickly. I urge that more loans be made available, not necessarily residences for the university, but for university professors and others who wish to build their own homes in various parts of the city. There are many areas of Canada in the same position. There are areas in which great mining development is taking place, such as those areas in Saskatchewan where potash is being mined. There are many such areas as I have mentioned.
I am not so sure that money is so tight, because one member of the government the Secretary of State wants to spend $6 million to buy a painting for the National Art Gallery. That $6 million would build 300 $20,000 homes or 600 $10,000 homes. How tight can money be when people on the government front benches can talk in terms like that? If money is scarce maybe it is time we began operating on a priority basis. I think No. 1 on the list of priorities would be to put a roof over a man's head and give him a place in which to live. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, if this situation is not corrected, before long people are going to be living in tents. That is how bad it is becoming in some areas of the country.
If we are going to give some thought to a priority basis perhaps we should consider how easy it is at present to get loans to buy cars, appliances, and for travel at a time when money is being curtailed for loans to allow a man to build a home for his wife and family.
I am concerned about the married man with small children who may be earning $85 to $100 a week. Where is this fellow going to live? He cannot get into an apartment house because in many cases they do not accept young families. He cannot rent a house because there is a shortage of such accommodation. This is a mighty serious situation today and it applies in many areas across the country. At present I think those who desire to build, and need a loan, have to be in the $6,000 a year bracket, receiving about $120 per week income, in order to get a loan for a house costing approximately $18,000. It is a serious situation and needs every ounce of thought and research that we can give it.

May 16. 1966
Tight Money Policy
I would like to see the minister responsible for the National Housing Act give greater thought to research on building construction and supplies because I am sure there must be some cheaper way in which we can build. I am not seeking loans for speculator builders, but I am speaking for those people who really need a home, who have made an application, who have qualified and yet are told they cannot get a loan because there is a 15 per cent cutback in the amount available.
So, Mr. Speaker, I conclude by saying what I said at the beginning. I am happy to have had this opportunity to make these few remarks with respect to the curtailment of loans for building and with respect to the tight money policy which the Liberal government is imposing on the people of Canada. I am also happy to give my wholehearted support to the amendment before the house.

It seems rather odd that there would be $300 million available and that the provinces and municipalities would not make full use of it. We want them to make full use of it.
Perhaps I might mention an example in the city of Toronto and the riding I represent concerning the housing situation in Canada. The three levels of government have started an urban renewal project in my riding. It is amazing how much time it has taken to develop. One of the main reasons for the delay was the lack of consultation between the authorities in the interests of those who were being expropriated. One of the main problems these people are facing is that of compensation. The federal government took the easy position that it is only the banker, that it puts up the money and plays no part in awarding compensation.
The people feel that three elements should be embodied in compensation. Not only must there be consideration of the fair market
May 16, 1966

value, but also a relocation expense should be allowed. Then there is the compulsory taking aspect. At one time there was a 10 per cent allowance for this, but now it is not allowed. Judging from the experience we have had in Broadview, no wonder people are not jumping into some of these urban renewal projects. They are being offered prices which are at least 25 per cent below what they would have to pay for comparable homes in another area.
It is very disappointing when we see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) bringing forth his budget in which he asks for a reduction of 10 per cent in government building, and only a small reduction with regard to private capital in housing. The statement of the minister on May 3 with reference to the 15 per cent reduction in connection with direct loans for the year 1966 is very disturbing. When one looks at the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation report for the year 1965 he finds there were 166,565 housing starts compared to 165,658 for 1964, an increase of .5 per cent compared to 11.5 per cent in 1964 and 14.2 per cent in 1963.
It is obvious that the trend is downward, and this should not be. When you add the 15 per cent reduction this year, it becomes a very disturbing picture. As a new member I looked upon the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) as a man of concern and compassion. I happened to read an article concerning a speech he made in Toronto in December 1964, when he said:
For all the talk about what we intend to do, for all our efforts, nearly 100,000 Canadian families live every waking moment of their lives under housing conditions that are really appalling-a disgrace to the communities in which they reside. The same 100,000 families cannot find other accommodation on the open market at rents they can afford to pay, and 20 per cent of all our occupied dwellings have very primitive bathing and toilet facilities. This, I suggest, is real poverty.
And quite apart from the despair and degradation of blight and decay, these neglected areas impose an unnecessary drain on the civic economy. Municipal services and other facilities cost more to provide, while assessments must decline. The extra overhead is subsidized by the taxpayers of the entire municipality-assessments must be increased in good areas to offset diminishing tax revenues in the run-down neighbourhoods.
This is a statement made by the minister in 1964. You get the picture for 1965 of a .5 per cent increase, and now he is asking for a 15 per cent decrease from the 1965 picture. Not only that, but the cost of houses financed

under the act increased in 1965 as it has in each year since 1961 because of the increase in the price of materials and wages, and the high cost of land. In 1965 the average cost of an N.H.A house was $17,402 as compared to $16,478 in 1964, an increase of $924.
The president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in his report indicated that the average income of a borrower under an N.H.A. loan was $6,655; the average age was 35 years and the borrower had two children. How many Canadians earn $6,655 per year and can qualify for a loan under the provisions of this legislation? I suggest that these provisions are too restrictive.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
The ceiling on N.H.A. mortgages was increased from $15,600 to $18,000 last year. That is an increase of $2,400. The interest rate is now 6| per cent, having increased in the past years from 5 per cent. The interest rate on conventional loans now stands at 7| per cent, or 1 per cent higher.
The president of C.M.H.C. indicated that 65 per cent of all new houses were being financed by conventional loans from insurance and trust companies, whereas 35 per cent are financed through N.H.A. loans. It seems to me that this situation should be reversed, and that 65 per cent should be financed under N.H.A. and 35 per cent by conventional loans.
When one realizes that an individual who has a mortgage of $18,000 at an interest rate of 6j per cent would have to pay $1,200 per year in interest or, as the last speaker mentioned, if a worker earns $100 per week it represents three months' work per year, he must also realize that housing costs are too high. In most cases housing mortgages run for a period of from 20 to 30 years. A man now 40 years of age who wants to buy a home will be 60, 65 or 70 before he has paid for it, and will have paid twice the original cost of his house as a result of the high rates of interest.
The lack of a housing program on the part of the government gives little or no opportunity for elderly people to purchase houses. People who have reached the twilight years of their fife are being forced to live in rooms at high rents. The government should take the initiative to make sure that these senior citizens are taken care of in their latter years.
It is obvious that the average income in Canada today is so low that the majority of

Corporation, for a nation-wide housing program in order to take a great deal of the weight of responsibility off the shoulders of conventional lending institutions.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
If there were a war, I am sure that Canadians would not hesitate to contribute to such a worthy cause as housing. Housing has become an urgent problem and the government must take immediate steps to solve it. We must take immediate steps also not only with regard to new homes but also with regard to older homes. In the riding of Broadview, which I represent many of these folk who are being ousted because of the urban renewal project are people who range in age between 55 and 60. They do not want to go to the suburbs but want to buy city homes and are faced with 8 per cent mortgages. There is a duty on the government, especially with regard to people who are being replaced because of urban renewal projects, to give them interest rates no greater than 64 per cent. This is something that should be done, and done immediately.
As the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) said, the way housing is financed in Toronto today is that you get a valuation of 87 per cent on the house and you have to pay a very high interest rate of 8 per cent. You also have to pay a 2 per cent insurance fee, plus an application fee and a legal fee. Is it any wonder that Canadians are unable to buy homes these days?
One final word, Mr. Speaker, and it is with regard to home improvement loans. The best defence that we can take with regard to blighted areas is to have homes in good repair. Under the National Housing Act loans were given to people for repairs. According to the report of the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, from 1961 to 1965 there has been a steady decline in home improvement loans. People should be encouraged to take these loans for home repairs because, as I said, the best defence we have against an area becoming blighted is to have homes in good repair. I could not help but agree with the hon. member for Northumberland, the former member for Broadview who certainly took a very active interest in constituency problems, when he said that Canadians deserve good homes. This gives them a sense of pride and achievement. These are the things we shoud work for, strive for, to make this a better Canada.

speechtext:
Although
it is very tempting, Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of entering into a controversy, even to the slightest degree, with my good friend the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) who was a little more belligerent tonight than he usually is, or even to discuss the preamble of the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) when introducing his amendment. I thought the young Conservatives were rather harsh with the former minister over the week end, particularly when one said to him, "This is the Pepsi generation, George, and you had better believe it". I suppose the hon. member for Northumberland, in referring back to incidents in 1956 and 1957 was only keeping pace with the type of attitude or atmosphere that has existed far too long in this particular house. I can be this sanctimonious about members referring to the past because I have not been here long enough to dig into the past and refer to each particular member, and some of the problems of a generation ago.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) who is responsible for the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, intends to speak before the debate is terminated tomorrow evening. I would prefer to leave it to him to refute some of the very thoughtful arguments which have been placed before us today, not only by the hon. member for Wellington South but also by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert). Looking through some of the clippings this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I find that statistics, for what they are worth, are reassuring to those members who are afraid that, as a result of the curtailment of money, there will not be as many housing starts this year as last year. I thought the hon. member for Broadview was rather pessimistic, so I should like to refer him to an editorial that appeared in the Globe and Mail on April 29.1 quote:
In the first place, although builders and members of parliament seem convinced that there will be a decrease in the number of houses built this year, the first quarter, in fact, shows an increase. Starts on single detached dwellings were up 18.9 per cent during the first three months of 1966 over 1965, and up 23.8 per cent in March over March of last year; and, as Mr. Nicholson pointed out, last year was the record year for house building.
I refer specifically to single dwelling homes, but I was interested in the remarks of

May 16, 1966
Tight Money Policy
the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, Mr. H. W. Hignett when he addressed the National House Builders Association and suggested that by 1970, 70 per cent of adult Canadians will be either in their twenties or older than 65, the ages of apartment dwellers. He left that association with the thought that perhaps the time had come for builders and the government to put the emphasis on a different style of home. Obviously by 1970 the plight of our senior citizens will be even more acute than it is today.
I think the recent report of the Senate committee on aging, which I believe is a rather historic document and one which will be to the everlasting credit of the Senators who worked on it, stresses the plight of the senior citizens of this country. Mr. Jean Lupien, vice president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation said to the same House Builders Association that they had become too dependant on government agencies for the flow of funds and that they were not meeting the real needs of Canadians for housing. Mr. Lupien is an expert in the field, and I am not. He says this:
You are trying to impose the wish for a house on people who cannot afford it. You put the houses away out where they create transportation costs for the buyers and you add to municipal problems.
I can only speak with some knowledge of my own community, Mr. Speaker. In a country as large as Canada, I realize that problems in the field of housing vary tremendously from area to area. I come from a province which should hang its head in shame, the province of Quebec, in so far as its approach to housing is concerned In this House of Commons, I represent the city of Verdun, a constituency of 90,000 people which has yet to build or stimulate the building or create the incentive for the co-operative building of even the first home of any description for senior citizens. I think it is a shame and it underlines one of the main problems which we have in a country made up of 11 different governments.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
In my community since 1962 I have been prodding the mayor and city council to take advantage of the terms offered by Central Mortgage, to no avail. In 1964, thanks to members in all parts of the house, I am sure, section 16A of the National Housing Act was amended to provide money by way of

loans up to 90 per cent of the purchase price of apartments, dwellings and homes for senior citizens and to those families of low income.
When that was done, once more I prodded my community to take advantage of this legislation, and I mention this because I am sure there are thousands of communities of which the same can be said. The 90,000 people of my constituency are concentrated in an area I could walk around in half an hour. They live in homes four or five storeys high, no less than three. The people live in rooms on $75 a month, in loneliness, in pathetic conditions, paying more than they can afford for a dingy room on the third floor.
Why is this so, Mr. Speaker? It is not because the federal government has not put the funds at the disposal of the provinces or the municipalities. It is not because Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has not been willing to place at the disposal of interested parties their assistance and experience. It is because there has not been sufficient pressure placed on municipalities at the civic level to take advantage of the legislation waiting here in Ottawa.
I can talk, of course, only of conditions in my own riding and I have no right to pass judgment on other ridings. I cannot cry at all for the fellow down the street who is having a hard time deciding whether to buy an $18,000 home or a $22,000 home. I cannot get too excited about him. I am concerned about the senior citizen who cannot find a flat for $40 a month and has to leave his or her spouse and move in with the children. These are the people I am concerned about, and I am concerned because I know that money to assist them is lying idle in Ottawa because through indifference, callousness or through ignorance of the fact that it is available, communities refuse to take advantage of it.
Some hon. members may ask, why not do something about it in your community? Well, Mr. Speaker, I did do something. About six or eight months ago, tired of the procrastination of the city council, I wrote every organization in the city of Verdun-service clubs, the Lions club, Kiwanis, the Richelieu club and senior citizens organizations. Finally I organized representatives from 30 of these bodies into a committee on housing. We then marched upon city hall a month before the civic elections and presented a brief requesting that the city of Verdun set up a housing committee consisting of eight people, four
May 16, 1S66

representing the city and four representing the citizens, in order that we might eventually stir the community or the municipality into action and request relief from the federal government under section 16A of the National Housing Act. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that in this venture we were successful. Our brief has been read, council has acted upon it and the committee has been set up. Central Mortgage and Housing has been contacted.
The procedure, Mr. Speaker, is rather laborious because this civic housing committee must now contact provincial authorities to make sure that it does not become involved in one of these federal-provincial disputes, but eventually a request for housing for senior citizens in my community will come to Ottawa to be, I hope, approved, provided certain norms are met.
I am not interested in giving this government or the previous government credit; credit is not important. But when we talk about housing for senior citizens, when we talk about slum clearance or when we talk about urban redevelopment, I think Canadians must realize that the responsibility for the implementation of much of the legislation in connection therewith falls upon their shoulders, as well as on the shoulders of the hon. member for Verdun, or the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales), or the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), or any other fine gentleman in this house.
I know, Mr. Speaker, there are certain communities, such as those like the city of Hamilton, certain sections of Toronto and probably some out west, which have taken advantage of the assistance offered by Central Mortgage to help our senior citizens. But hundreds and thousands of Canadians, according to the Senate report on aging, are living in conditions that are a shame to Canada, with our tremendous standard of living. This state of affairs is not brought about by a government unwilling to do anything to correct it: The fault lies in the red tape which exists between federal, provincial and civic authorities, which prevents our walking into a community and saying that we should knock down 25 blocks square and build some decent housing for the citizens. This type of initiative must come from the civic level.
Many of the provinces have already realized that this should be the approach, and at
Tight Money Policy
least four or five of them have supplemented the assistance offered in worthy cases. The province of Quebec is probably the most backward of all provinces in this regard, but there are indications that in the very near future that province will be setting up an association or department similar to that existing in Ontario and in other provinces.
However, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether private builders, who have had the best of both worlds for so many years now, with housing shortages and ample funds from private industry, private enterprise, other private sources and from the government, have really done their part in the matter of funds. Looking around some of the communities close to Verdun and some of the housing projects which have been constructed, it does not take very much vision to foresee the slums of the future. It seems to me that a review of housing in general is needed. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has been the ideal man to look after Central Mortgage. I do not know who chases whom, but it came under his jurisdiction when he was postmaster general, and it is again under his jurisdiction now that he is Minister of Labour.
The minister pointed out the other day that we were cutting back funds by 15 per cent, not over the average of the last five years, but 15 per cent of a record year. I do not think in all fairness that the government should be chastised for adopting such a policy. The members who have spoken so far have spoken well, but their comments have been made really in a different light. The hon. member for Broadview, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso) and the hon. member for Wellington South have pointed to a social illness, namely the lack of housing in general, which I do not think is tied in too much with interest rates. I think this question is tied in with the logical profit-making attitude of private industry. I believe it is time for the government to give more directives and more incentives to build the type of housing I envisage, the type of housing which the president of Central Mortgage and also the vice president politely pointed out is so badly needed now, and will be even more badly needed by 1970.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
In certain communities such as mine, the people cannot afford the luxury of a nice home in the country with a lot 50 x 50, a garden, and all the rest of it. That sort of

May 16, 1966
Tight Money Policy
thing might be the dream of the young executive who can afford it. It cannot be the dream of our senior citizens in the community in which I live.
This is why I am pleased that the government, in its policy of restraint respecting tight money, has been very careful not to curtail the moneys available for these types of enterprises which have to do with senior citizens.
I am saddened that the municipalities across this country, either through lack of communication, indifference, or callousness, have not faced up to the responsibilities they have toward the citizens of their communities. These responsibilities should not rest on the shoulders of the federal government alone. They must be met through co-operation between the civic, provincial and federal levels of government.
I thought when the federal government made changes in the National Housing Act, granting up to 90 per cent coverage on loans on projects dedicated to providing housing for senior citizens, and also those with low incomes, that there would have been generated the biggest building boom in the housing history of Canada. That has not happened. Frankly, why it has not happened has puzzled people who are close to the problems of senior citizens. It has puzzled those who are active in the field of social welfare-such as volunteer workers, or the members of the Victorian Order of Nurses-who day in and day out see the dilapidated conditions under which senior citizens live, many of them paying $50 or $60 a month for a room on the island of Montreal because no other type of housing is available. That sort of thing is a sin; it is a shame. The responsibility is not entirely that of the federal government. It falls simply on the shoulders of the citizens of those communities, who are responsible for citizens less fortunate than they are.
Those are the people who refuse to march on city council demanding housing for senior citizens. They do not send resolutions to the provincial government asking it to get in touch with the federal government and ask for money- money which is waiting for them and which, as I understand, although I have no statistics in front of me, has never been used to its fullest extent. There has never been pressure on the government to expand these types of funds because they have never come anywhere near to being completely used by communities for the purposes I speak of.

I know what I have done in my community. I know what we shall be doing for our senior citizens in our community. But I do not think it is my duty as a federal member of parliament to have to generate interest on the civic level about the things I speak of. I believe that the role of the members of this house is to provide the plan, the money and the know-how. People all across Canada should take a look at their own communities, at their own church group, at their own social groups, and perhaps ask themselves; "I wonder what conditions that old gentleman who has just passed us lives under? Does he live in a room? Why is there no housing in our community? Why are there not homes for senior citizens around here?
I might add, Mr. Speaker, it is not because money is not available; it is not because the know-how is not there; it is not because the builders are not there. It is because in this big country in which we live, where you have federal, provincial and civic administrations all working very delicately together, all afraid to step on each other's toes, we have to start with requests on the civic level, going up the ladder to the provincial government, and then to the federal government.
I resist the temptation to answer some of the very pointed, and at times logical questions that were raised in this debate. I will leave that pleasant chore for the minister tomorrow evening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of saying a few words on this supply motion. Why is that, Mr. Speaker? The answer is simple. I want to talk about certain specific policies and situations designed and created by this government.
May 16. 1966



The three legs of the stool that have brought about the present situation are, first, the supply of money. Second, the demand for loan money, and third, out of the interplay between these two, the interest rate.
This government's policy has been one-sided, having to do with the supply of money. First of all you have the statement by the Minister of Finance about paying 5 per cent on taxes taken, with the promise that this would be paid back later. That is a policy to dry up the supply of lendable funds. There is no doubt about it. Then there are other policies, such as those implemented by the Minister of Labour who is responsible for central mortgage and housing, which are responsible for raising the mortgage rate of National Housing Act mortgages from 6J per cent to 6J per cent.
Anyone who has watched the result of this action-and I have seen its results in my area-knows that for many people it is hard to find lendable funds. In many cases they have been unable to find them. Many people have deferred their plans to build because of raised interest rates, which have cut the demand for lendable funds. People who do not believe that are like the ostrich which puts its head in the sand.
I notice that the Minister of Fisheries shakes his head. I would ask him, how many fishermen would go fishing, and would buy boats, and so on, if the interest rate on the things they had to buy went up, up and up? They would not engage in fishing because they would not be able to figure where they could come out with a profit. After all, they are all economic men; that is, they are out to make a profit. If they feel that they cannot make money, they will not be induced to work. Similarly, rising interest rates mean a lower demand for lendable funds. Those funds have been curtailed. All that stems from what this government has done. In other words, money for housing has been deliberately dried up.
There are other things to be considered. Take bank loans as an example. Banks are not interested at the present time in making small bank loans because of the shortage of funds. They can make much larger loans, however, at the 6 per cent rate. So when the small businessman comes along and wants a loan; they way, "No, we just have not got the
Tight Money Policy
money". The banker cannot tell the businessman exactly why he is not making the loan to him.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The banker will tell him that his security is not good, his chances of making a profit are not good, or something of that sort. In 1962 this government had an election platform which included a policy and program to help small business. Let me read exactly what they said they would do to help small business. They said they would ensure a square deal for small business; they said that Libera] policies were for more plentiful credit, lower taxes and expanding business; they said that economic measures would be designed to broaden opportunities for the various enterprises of our smaller manufacturers, retailers and service businesses.
Has this government forgotten its promise of 1962, or has it changed its mind? This was their platform in 1962. Now they are doing just the opposite. I was amazed by the statement of the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey). He said he had prodded different local people to bring into effect certain policies for housing, old age pensions, and so on. He said he had prodded and prodded them and still had not been able to get them to act. Did the hon. member ever consider that there was a more serious fault than people in local communities suffering from inertia? Unless you implement over-all policies, which this government has never done, you will not get the proper reaction from local people. I will refer to this election campaign propaganda a little later on.
I draw attention to this three-legged stool; the supply of money on one side, the demand for loans on another, and the interplay of both creating a higher interest rate. In the result the interest rate goes up. What you are doing in these circumstances is closing off those people who want loans to purchase consumer goods, thereby preventing putting this money back into the process of production and producing goods for export. You head off inflation but the economy suffers; there is no question about that.
This government has restricted the supply of money. As a result our people are crying out for consumer goods and there are not enough consumer goods to go around. That is the interrelationship effect on our economy of increasing the interest rate. I suspect that the government has raised the interest rate on

May 16, 1966
Tight Money Policy
Central Mortgage and Housing loans from 6J per cent to 6J per cent because they intend to amend the Bank Act to raise the 6 per cent interest on bank loans. I am waiting for them to do this, and I have both barrels cocked if they do.
The raising of the 6 per cent interest rate on bank loans will not solve the present economic ills of this country, because we have in our economy certain rigidities; we have a monopolistic economy wherein competition is not the same between different groups. I can prove my point by simply saying that you may have perfect competition, for example, between one large number of producers. To illustrate my point I would refer to our farmers who produce wheat; one farmer does not realize that his neighbour, also producing wheat, is in competition with him. In other words, there is perfect competition between these farmers. This is a term that economists use and it applies to two farmers, for instance, each of whom does not know that the other is a competitor.
This is a vastly different situation to that applying to the eight chartered banks we have in this country. I may go into one bank and borrow money from them, but have dealings with another bank. I may talk to one bank manager and indicate that I paid so much interest in another bank. I do not know whether banks circulate this information among themselves, but they find out these things-there are many ways in which this can be done-and there is an interchange of views. At various dinners, for example, they get together, or while at their clubs, and find out what the other is charging as interest on loans, and that sort of thing; then they make reports periodically.
Therefore you have a degree of monopolistic competition in the banking industry of this country. I would point out to the house that what will work among farmers will not work among banks. If you start raising the interest rate beyond 6 per cent, you will generate with regard to the banks of this country the demand for reform. There may be pressure upon parliament to bring in a new measure to take over the supply of lendable money. An element in the west will be saying that the Bank of Canada should take over the lending function of our chartered banks. I am not one of those who advocates this being done, but this will be suggested; make no mistake about that. The

Bank of Canada, as everyone knows, is the fountain-head for funds, with the exception of deposits. It stimulates deposits by lending money to the chartered banks, and they in turn extend credit to around twelve times the funds they have borrowed. When those funds are re-deposited in the banks, they lend them again at the expanded rate, and so the cycle continues. This is how the banks receive their lendable funds.
If the ceiling on the interest rate is removed and banks are allowed to charge more than 6 per cent, we will be breaking faith with an undertaking given to the people of this country a good many years ago, that the interest rate would be 6 per cent. This will be evidence of the fact that this government has not the capacity or know-how to control our economy without raising the interest rate and placing a heavier burden upon the man who wishes to own a house. He will be paying a much higher rate of interest on his mortgage money and, being a small borrower, will not be able to borrow more money. I hope the government will bear these facts in mind and think twice before they embark upon a policy such as the raising of the interest rate on bank loans.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Let us spend a few moments considering the effect of this tight money policy. There is no doubt that it is a tight money policy. The government is restricting the supply of money, by one means or another, by government measures and edicts, and that is curtailing the expansion of the economy. There is now a greater demand for the money that is available, and so interest rates rise. It is like a dog chasing its tail. Everybody wants more money and pays higher interest rates. The only check is when interest rates climb so high that nobody can afford to borrow because they will not make a profit. Consequently they do without. That is not what we want in our economy.
Look at the cost-of-living index. Everything is costing more, whether for production or consumption. The housewife knows what she has to pay when she goes to the store. There has never been such a rapid rise in the cost of living as there has been since this government took office. The D.B.S. statistics clearly illustrate this.
The value of the dollar has depreciated in relation to purchasing power. The old age
May 16, 1S66

pension of $75 a month is now worth about only $70 in terms of purchasing power. My hon. friend from Verdun was shedding crocodile tears for the old people, but he did not tell us that the rising cost of living is taking the bread out of their mouths and cutting their standard of living from under them. There are thousands of others, retired civil servants and people on fixed incomes, who are terribly hurt by the rise in the cost of living.
Rising costs are also affecting those who manufacture goods for export. I have talked to many of them in my part of the country and they tell me they are being priced out of foreign markets. Markets which they enjoyed for years are diminishing, simply because of high costs.
It is not so long ago since we concluded the Columbia river deal. Today I was amazed to hear the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Pepin), who represents the constituency of Drummond-Arthabaska, in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), saying that the funds which have been received from the United States to build Columbia river dams had accumulated certain interest. Those of us who studied the treaty had this figured out. The minister also said that a portion of these funds had been spent, but he did not tell us whether the money which was received from the United States to build these dams will now be sufficient in view of inflation, the rise in the cost of consumer goods and all the other things that make up the costs of production.
He simply told us that interest had accumulated. I did not rise in my place to criticize him because I did not ask the question, but I can assure the hon. member for Kootenay West that if he looks at the minister's answer in Hansard he will find it was no answer at all to his question.

speechtext:
I do not have the past figures on C.M.H.C. loans, and in order to answer the question fully it would be necessary to cover all the adjoining factors. I was here at the time, but the two situations are not comparable. Furthermore, more money was put into housing at that time than is the case at present. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud) thinks he has a point and he is trying to save what he could call the good name and good policies of his government. I do not want to get sidetracked on an across-the-floor question, but there were different factors then as compared with now. The former government never embarked upon a policy of introducing tight money, not to the extent that the present government is doing. The two situations are completely non-comparable.
o (9:30 p.m.)
Coming back to the Liberal program as outlined in the general election of 1962, I should like to go into the field of community development and housing, because different members have spoken on this particular subject. I should like to place on the record what the Liberal party had in mind in 1962, and then we will see how much of that they have carried out. They said they would set up, if a Liberal government were elected, a municipal loan fund which, working with the provinces, would provide money for needed municipal services. They said:
We need better streets and roads to reduce traffic congestion, less pollution, more parks. A great backlog of needed projects is held up for lack of municipal financing. The fund will make loans for sound municipal improvements which provincial governments approve but for which capital is unobtainable on reasonable terms from existing Canadian sources.
Noble thoughts; but how much has been done. The hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) was lamenting the fact that nothing had been done in his community. This is what they said they would do when they were fighting an election. Let me read the next one. They said they would clear slums and renew blighted areas of our cities and

May 16. 1966
Tight Money Policy
towns. This is how they explained what they would do. They said:
Federal grants for urban renewal projects will be extended in scope and increased in amount. This is essential to civic progress in many areas.
How much of this was ever done? May I say, very little. Here is the next promise to the people. They were going to increase the low rental homes. Here is what they said they were going to do:
New homes for rent are the positive side of slum clearance. A new Liberal government will join with the provinces and municipalities in a major campaign. It will give special attention to the housing needs of old-age pensioners.
What did my hon. friend from Verdun say? He said that nothing had been built for old age pensioners. Here they fought an election and put out bait to try to get the old age pensioners to vote for them. Do you think they will ever vote for them again? This is what they said in 1962. Have they forgotten what they said in 1962; have they changed their minds? Different speakers on the government side already have said in this evening's debate that nothing had been done in respect of low rental housing; that is, that there has been no program to bring that into being, nor has there been a program of homes for the aged.
I like to put this on the record, because these things are coming back to haunt this government. They should be put on the record because the members of the government have forgotten about them. They said that if they were elected in 1962, they would extend national housing legislation to provide N.H.A. insured mortgages for the purchase of existing homes as well as for building new homes. They said that this broadening, under proper safeguards, would enable more Canadians to become home owners. What are they doing now? They are raising the interest rates from 6J per cent to 6f per cent. This is just the opposite to what they said they were going to do.
Here is another one, and in this case they even are trying to get the farmer's vote. They said they would improve rural housing:
A new Liberal government will bring to national housing policy the flexibility in planning, standards and finance necessary to meet the varied needs of different areas.
They said they are going to help the farmers with their homes. How much have they done? There are a lot of poor farm homes in

my area and I have not seen any benefits there. It is just another gimmick. I have here a document of several pages. I could read many extracts setting forth different policies of this government, but one is as futile as the other. This is the 1962 platform of the Liberal party. I am not trying to pull the wool over your eyes; I am trying to take wool off your eyes, and off the eyes of the public so that they will see exactly what this government has been doing in respect of carrying out its pledges which it made to the people.
Now, in concluding my remarks, I should like to say that what is needed is the creation of a condition in the economy so that jobs will be available and so that everyone can earn a little money in order to purchase consumer goods. At the same time there should be an adequate supply of goods so that prices can be kept in check and so that there will be a proper balance between supply and demand for mortgage funds, and supply and demand in respect of the goods which are available.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to ask the house to reject the amendment proposed by the official opposition, I feel I must start by pointing out that, contrary to what seems to have been suggested by members of the official opposition until now, looking at when they had the opportunity to alleviate the problems of which they speak, their record certainly does not justify their asking for the support of this house or this country for the amendment they have put forward. I presume they have put it forward under the guise of a suggestion that they have a greater capability to deal with the problems of housing which still remain in this country than has the government.
It is interesting to note that in 1962 housing starts totalled only 130,095; in 1963 they jumped to 148,624, and from there, in 1964, they jumped to 165,658. Finally we find that in 1965 there were 166,565 housing starts. In other words, in less than four years there has been an increase of 22 per cent.

maintopic: DINNER RECESS DURING DISCUSSION OF SUPPLY MOTION

speechtext: May I ask a question of the hon. member.

speechtext:
I would be happy to answer questions when I have completed my remarks. It is not my habit to make an extended speech. If time does permit, I would be happy to answer questions for my hon. friend or for any of my colleagues in this house.
May 16. 1966

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this dramatic improvement did not come about merely by chance. My colleague the hon. member tor Hamilton West (Mr. Macaluso)- the distinguished chairman of the transport committee-I thought outlined most effectively the measures which have been put into effect by this government to stimulate the building of homes generally and to stimulate activity throughout this country in an effort to deal with the problem of supplying proper housing for the older people and people on low incomes. He also outlined our efforts in the field of urban renewal.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I think the measures of the type to which he referred, including the provision for 90 per cent financing of low rental public housing, increased federal funds for urban renewal and, contrary to what was suggested by the hon. member who just spoke, making N.H.A. loans available for older homes, provided they are located in urban renewal areas, have all had a lot to do with the very important increase in housing starts since this government took office. There has been a dramatic increase in the supply of funds available through the federal government for urban renewal and low rental housing. This, as well as many other measures, has contributed to this improvement.
If I refer to a particular example of one community in this country of ours I think it will help illustrate what I am trying to say about this difference which has come about since this government has had an opportunity to bring in measures to increase the amount of housing available for Canadians. In my own community of Windsor in 1962 there were only 495 units started. In 1963 this number increased to 728; in 1964 to 1,125 and in 1965 to some 1,800. It is interesting to note that in 1965 for the first time housing starts reached a total greater than the 1,700 which occurred in 1954. In other words, when our hon. friends in the official opposition were in office and had charge of the housing policy of this country, just taking the period from 1959 to 1963, in the Windsor area the annual total averaged between 500 and 700 units as compared with the prospective 2,000 starts for 1966. There are some 695 publicly owned low rental units either under construction now or to be started within the next several weeks. I think some of the measures of this government to which I referred have had a very
Tight Money Policy
important effect in bringing about this improvement in the Windsor area.
Reference has been made by various speakers to the effect of the present government's policy on the housing picture for the current year. It seems to me that it should be emphasized that this government has made it clear that it does not intend to reduce the number of direct loans to be made available to the home building industry this year. Last year some 31,500 direct loans were made available for the construction and purchase of homes. The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has stressed in this house that the government program for this year will not reduce that number below that level.
It should be remembered that of the 166,000 starts in 1965 the majority were financed by private lenders. If the prospect in this country at this time indicates that this record level of starts may be reduced by 15 per cent this coming year the blame for this decrease must fall upon private lenders who are not carrying out a definite social responsibility of providing loans at the same level.
I do not agree with those hon. members who have suggested that the Minister of Labour has announced that this government has decreed a 15 per cent cutback in housing starts in Canada for 1966. I read the minister's statement and as far as I can see he merely conveyed to this house the latest information available in relation to projections for housing starts in the current year. I hope that the final result of construction programs financed through either direct loans from C.M.H.C. or through private lenders will not be less than the record number of starts in 1965. At the same time I cannot help but note that there are areas in this country, including the Windsor area, which at the present time still have a serious housing shortage. The efforts of this government since it took office have helped to begin to fill the gaps which exist in housebuilding in areas such as Windsor where a serious need still exists.
The very important and significant increase in employment in the Windsor area since 1963 has created an additional pressure on the limited supply of housing available at the beginning of this period of improvement in economic conditions. I suggest this improvement in the economy of this area is a direct result of some of the economic programs implemented by this government, including the designated area measure and the automotive pact.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
At this time I should like to call upon the minister and this government to develop and put into effect as quickly as possible policies and programs which will give special attention to the needs of areas such as Windsor in order that these housing needs will not remain unfilled in the immediate future. I am sure the minister will do everything possible to encourage private lenders to become more actively engaged in the housing field. If his efforts, by way of what I might call morale suasion, are not successful in bringing to their minds a sense of responsibility the government will have to give active consideration to a greater direct involvement in the mortgage financing field.
At the present time the government should take steps to give special attention through its program of direct lending to such areas as Windsor. Special attention should be given to the creation of quotas greater than those which might otherwise be available in those areas which have a special need for housing. I must stress that this need would have been much worse at this time had it not been for the efforts of this government under the leadership provided by the hon. Minister of Labour. This government in making efforts through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and through co-operation with municipal and provincial governments to find an answer to these needs.
The time has also come when we must encourage private industry to take a more active part in providing housing for their employees.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
This is not merely a matter of responsibility on the part of those industries to the communities in which they find themselves. Surely, in areas such as Windsor it is also in the direct interests of the industries in question to make certain that they are able to keep the skilled working force they have, to attract additional workers to fill the jobs that are being created in large part because of the success of the economic policies of this government. I think that the minister, both directly and through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, should encourage the major industrial firms in communities like Windsor, either to do something themselves in the field of housing for their employees or to combine together to form non-profit corporations which, with the assistance of Central

Mortgage in planning and perhaps in financing if necessary, would help fill the demand for housing in areas such as the one from which I come.
Another point I should like to make at this time, Mr. Speaker, is that I feel the income scale now being imposed by the Ontario Housing Corporation on new public housing projects, which are being constructed in areas such as Windsor, has a definite need of revision. I feel that a study of this scale will indicate that the penalty rent level comes in to play too quickly and fails to take into account the realities of the wages that people who work in our factories actually earn today, as well as the costs they have to meet out of those wages. I recognize that the principle is that people above a certain income level are to be discouraged through the application of the rental scale from staying in those units. They are thus being encouraged to go into the private housing market. At the present time, however, in many areas of this country, there is a shortage of private housing for these people. It either does not exist or if it exists at all, is at a rental which is difficult for factory workers or other people in that type of job to meet. I think that equity and the needs of the people in the lower income ranges demands a revision of this income scale on the part of those concerned.
I have not hesitated to speak in a way which might be taken by some to contain a note of criticism of those responsible for our housing policy, perhaps not criticism so much as calling for further action in certain directions. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I want to stress again my feeling that, in spite of this call for further action I can at the same time ask this house to reject this amendment offered by the official opposition. I say this because of the record of achievement of the present government, which I feel justifies all hon. members in this house in having a feeling of confidence that this government is capable of continuing to meet the needs that still exist for better housing for our citizens in every part of this country. Because of this confidence on my part, because of the evidence on which this confidence is based, I feel that the amendment offered is not well founded when it, in effect, criticizes the government for bringing about difficulties in the availability of funds.
I reiterate that we have reached the point where there must be a development and a
May 16, 1966	COMMONS
putting into effect of policies under which special consideration is given to areas which still have a serious need of housing. At the same time I feel that the achievements to which I have referred are such that this house is obliged to vote against this amendment, to continue to support this government so it can continue to move ahead to deal with the housing problems that still remain in a way in which I am sure they are able to do, based on the clear record of their period in office.

Mr. Speaker, on May 12 I asked the minister the following question:
In view of press reports that there will be an over-expenditure of some $200 million on the Columbia treaty projects before they are completed, would the minister inform the house whether any reports from the federal representative on the fed-eral-British Columbia liaison committee, or from the federal representative on the joint engineering board, indicate that the projects will cost considerably more than the government of British Columbia has received from the United States under the terms of the Columbia treaty?
My question is based on newpaper reports and other information I have obtained from British Columbia sources with respect to two things: first, faulty engineering studies and, second, the anticipated cost of other Columbia treaty projects with respect to faulty engineering studies, I wish to quote from the Nelson Daily News for February 24, 1966:
Vancouver sources reported Wednedsay that the construction schedule at the dam has been hard hit by inaccuracies in engineering data supplied to the dam builders. Core drillings reportedly showing solid bed rock proved false when the underlying structures were found to be weakened by dirt seams and cracks.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I was rather surprised to read this report in view of the fact that the engineers of the federal water resources branch appeared before the standing committee on external affairs when it was giving consideration to the Columbia river treaty and protocol in April, 1964 and stated they had every confidence in the engineering studies undertaken by the water resources branch, their counterparts in British Columbia, and the various engineering consulting firms.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
I just want to quote briefly from the Revelstoke Review. Mr. Strachan, when addressing a public meeting, had this to say:
When the Columbia treaty was signed the government claimed $273 million paid for downstream benefits would be invested and with accumulated interest would total $501 million in 1973. Mr. Strachan said this was supposed to pay the cost of three dams and one half the cost of generators at Mica Creek.
"Because of this we went ahead with High Arrow, which will flood good farm land and probably wreck some fine sport fishing," he said. "Now we find that this will not provide enough money, and that the people will have to find the balance."
May 16. 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Many people in British Columbia are concerned about this information, which appeared in several newspapers in the province.
In the first instance, I was surprised to find, in view of the project cost estimates submitted by the water resources branch, to be found at page 185 of No. 3, Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence, Standing Committee on External Affairs, as submitted by the water resources branch, that these preliminary cost estimates used in making evaluations were made by the water resources branch and its engineering consultants.
I was also surprised, Mr. Speaker, in view of the evidence given by Mr. G. M. MacNabb of the water resources branch, to be found at page 248 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence given before the Standing Committee on External Affairs on Friday, April 10, 1964, in which he said:
At the end of the construction period you will see that we have a surplus of $53 million in 1973, after paying all construction costs over that period.
I was also surprised in view of the evidence given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs before the standing committee on external affairs, during the course of which he was asked this question:
